---
title: "Origins"
---

The zotQDA ecosystem came into being at the end of July 2026, during the
JCrete unconference (27 to 31 July 2026) on Crete and the JCrete
"afterglow" that followed it.

Attending JCrete is formally "holiday" — an (un)conference I attend of my
own accord and at my own expense —, yet to me it is one of the densest,
most productive and most inspiring weeks of the whole year.

## A session on the future of teaching

[JCrete](https://jcrete.org) is an unconference: there is no programme in
advance; the participants put the programme together themselves every
morning. On 28 July 2026 I ran a session there on the future of teaching:
**"What to teach and how"**. The session, and what became of it, are
documented in the conference repository:
[JCrete 2026](https://github.com/JCrete/jcrete2026).

The zotQDA ecosystem (zotQDA, qdaZ, qdaPy and qdaR) grew out of that
session — out of the realisation that I lacked the tool to widen and
deepen the session's brainstorming after the conference: through
interviews with experienced people from software development, followed by
qualitative content analysis.

## The missing piece

The need is older than the conference. In my main job I lead the teaching
of a research focus at a medical faculty. I want curriculum development to
rest on evidence rather than opinions, and that evidence is qualitative to
a large extent: free-text answers from evaluations, conversations with
students and teachers, examination reports, literature. Anyone who wants
to analyse such material systematically ends up at qualitative content
analysis — and needs a tool for it.

There is no shortage of tools. There I have MAXQDA at my disposal as
licensed software, probably one of the leading programs in the
German-speaking world, and the [comparison page](comparison.qmd) makes it
plain: MAXQDA and ATLAS.ti can do considerably more than this ecosystem.
That they were still out of the question for me has three reasons.

First, they are **proprietary programs**, and those are out of the
question for me in the context of scientific work: I am an advocate of
*reproducible and open research* — data and analysis tool must be freely
accessible, with the lowest possible hurdles. Years ago I therefore moved
all my analyses from SPSS and niche software such as VectorNTI to **R**
and **Python**, and with the freedom, the flexibility and quality of the
analyses grew as well.

Second, they are **monolithic**, with project files of their own. That can
be an advantage, especially for less IT-minded and inexperienced users;
for computing-minded users and professionals, in my experience the
**modular UNIX principle** proves itself: an ecosystem of specialised
tools that can be combined at will and are therefore equal to even the
most complex tasks.

Third, they stand *beside* the reference manager, not *inside* it. My
material has long been living in Zotero: PDFs, notes, highlights, all
sorted and tagged. And Zotero, as a powerful open-source reference
manager, already brings almost everything qualitative content analysis
needs: a reader with annotations, comments, notes and tags,
synchronisation across operating systems, a web interface, and group
libraries for working as a team. So why reinvent the wheel? The thought
was no bigger than the question why I should really go somewhere else to
code — a Zotero plugin is the logical consequence.

## JCrete's hacking space

JCrete's hacking space is nothing more than the rooms of the Orthodox
Academy of Crete after the last session of the day. A terrace overlooking
the sea, several plain rooms with tables, a few chairs and — far too
scarce — power sockets. The magic ingredient is the participants, who
work on things of their own but also look over your shoulder when you are
stuck. For a first version that is the right environment: you can build
something, show it to somebody, and work their answer in the same day.

The oldest parts of **zotQDA** came into being on the very day of the
session **"What to teach and how"**. As JCrete 2026 went on, the core
took shape — a code is a mark on a Zotero annotation, the code system is
a note, and both stay readable even when the plugin is removed again.
That was exactly the idea: no project file that can get lost or become
unreadable.

## The echo

At home, from 5 August on, in the evenings and at weekends, the two
analysis libraries **qdaR** and **qdaPy** joined. Two, because R and
Python are the undisputed pair of modern data analysis — and because the
same calculation in two independent languages, plus the JavaScript plugin
qdaZ, is an ideal touchstone: where the versions diverge, a bug is
rarely far away. Cross-validation did in fact surface several errors
that a single implementation would never have revealed.

## What that means for zotQDA

There is no funder, no commission and no fixed schedule.

The tools do exactly the things I have painfully missed myself, and
delegate everything else to established open-source software: Whisper
does the recording, ELAN the annotation of audio and video, Zotero the
library, R and Python the statistics.

For years I have profited from other people's open-source software. The
zotQDA ecosystem lets me give something back to the community, and it is
therefore released under the AGPL with an additional permission making
clear that the results belong to the researchers.

## What comes next

Slowly, and in this order: coding first, then text analysis, then the two
libraries for R and Python, audio and video last. What is done is in
[Features](features.qmd); what is missing is listed right beside it.

If you use the tool in your own work, I would be glad to hear from you —
especially about the places where it does not yet work the way it should.
